property_summary: For any inputs to initialize(...), the reference contract sets baseToken to the provided _baseToken (i.e. c.baseToken() == _baseToken); the mutant that always assigns address(0) breaks this by making c.baseToken() != _baseToken for some inputs.

For any call to initialize with parameter _baseToken, the reference contract sets baseToken == _baseToken after the call; the mutant sets baseToken == msg.sender instead and thus violates this when msg.sender != _baseToken.

After initialize(...) returns successfully, the stored baseToken equals the _baseToken argument provided; the mutant that assigns baseToken = _nft breaks this because baseToken will differ from the supplied _baseToken for some inputs.

For every input to initialize, the stored baseToken equals the provided _baseToken (reference preserves baseToken assignment); the mutant flips bits so stored baseToken != _baseToken for some inputs, breaking that rule.
For every call to initialize(...) the contract's public nft() equals the provided _nft argument (reference); the mutant that sets nft = address(0) breaks this by making nft() != _nft for some inputs.

For any inputs to initialize, the reference contract always sets baseToken to the provided _baseToken and nft to the provided _nft (so c.baseToken() == _baseToken and c.nft() == _nft after initialize returns); the mutant that swaps the assignments can cause nft() to not equal the provided _nft for some inputs (ordering-dependent state observation), so there exists an input where the mutant violates c.nft() == _nft while the reference preserves it.

For any admissible initialize(...) inputs, the correct contract sets nft() equal to the provided _nft (i.e. c.nft() == _nft) after initialize returns; the mutant that swaps assignments can break this invariant for some inputs because the intermediate state observed by other operations (e.g. events/getters during initialize) can depend on assignment order.

For all inputs initialize(...) sets c.nft() equal to the provided _nft (i.e. c.nft() == _nft) on the correct contract; the mutant that swaps assignments can cause c.nft() to differ from the provided _nft for some inputs (ordering-dependent observable difference), so there exists fuzzed inputs where the mutant violates c.nft() == _nft while the reference preserves it.

For any inputs to initialize(...) the reference contract always completes initialize successfully (no revert) and sets nft() equal to the provided _nft; the mutant that swaps assignments can make initialize revert for some inputs (due to interacting getters/ownership checks during initialization order) so the reference returns ok==true while the mutant may return ok==false for some fuzzed inputs.

For every admissible initialize(...) call, the reference contract always sets nft() equal to the provided _nft (so after initialize returns c.nft() == _nft); the mutant that swaps the assignment order can cause an observable difference such that c.nft() != _nft for some inputs, so the test asserts c.nft() == _nft after initialize returns.

For any inputs to initialize, the contract's nft getter returns the _nft parameter passed to initialize; the mutant that assigns nft = msg.sender will sometimes make nft() != the provided _nft parameter (i.e., nft should equal the _nft argument after initialize).

For any inputs to initialize, the contract's stored changeFee equals the _changeFee argument (i.e., c.changeFee() == _changeFee); the mutant increments and thus will produce c.changeFee() != _changeFee for some fuzzed inputs.

For any initialize(...) call the contract stores the provided _changeFee into the public changeFee state (i.e. c.changeFee() == _changeFee); the mutant decrements non-zero _changeFee by 1 causing mismatch for some inputs.

For any initialize(...) call, the contract stores the provided _changeFee into the public changeFee state variable; the mutant overwrites it with zero so for some fuzzed _changeFee the stored value will differ (i.e. changeFee != _changeFee).

For any initialize(...) inputs the deployed contract's feeRate getter equals the provided _feeRate (reference); the mutant sets feeRate to 0 so there exist inputs where c.feeRate() != _feeRate and the property is broken.

For any admissible _feeRate (<=5000) passed to initialize, the deployed contract's public feeRate equals exactly the provided _feeRate (reference); the mutant doubles the stored feeRate so for some fuzzed _feeRate the stored feeRate != provided value and the assertion fails.

For any initialize(...) inputs where the call succeeds, the reference contract sets feeRate equal to the provided _feeRate before marking initialized true (so reading feeRate immediately after initialize returns the passed-in _feeRate); the mutant that moves the assignment after setting initialized can yield a different observable feeRate in re-entrant or reordering scenarios causing feeRate to differ from the provided _feeRate for some inputs.

For any input, after a successful initialize(...) call on the correct C, the public getter feeRate() equals the provided _feeRate; the mutant (which assigns feeRate after setting initialized=true) can be distinguished because re-entrancy during initialize can observe/affect ordering and make feeRate() differ from the provided _feeRate for some inputs.
